(AP Photo/Michael Probst, File) (AP Photo/Michael Probst) FRANKFURT, Germany (AP) — European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will resign nine months ahead of the end of her term, a move that opens the way for European leaders to choose a successor ahead of France's presidential election next year.
 Lagarde will leave Feb. 7, the ECB said Thursday. Her eight-year term was to end Oct. 31, 2027.
 The resignation opens the way for complex political horse trading over her successor and to fill the posts of two other top officials who are leaving next year.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement The announcement was not a surprise since there has been speculation that Lagarde would leave early to enable EU leaders to choose a successor while pro-EU French President Emmanuel Macron is still in office. That would guard against the possibility that right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen might win the election and influence the choice.
 "That she leaves early is no surprise and does not change the outlook for ECB policies," said Holger Schmieding, chief economist at Berenberg bank.
 European Council President Antonio Costa said that the selection process "will be initiated today and will proceed without delay."
 The term of another top ECB official — chief economist Philip Lane — is to end May 31, while another member of the ECB's executive board, Isabel Schnabel, is resigning at year end to move to the International Monetary Fund. European leaders are expected to work out a package deal to apportion the three vacancies among member countries in a complex round of political bargaining.
 Advertisement Advertisement EU leaders would likely seek to reach agreement on all three posts before a summit meeting on Dec. 17-18, said Holger Schmieding, chief economist at Berenberg bank.
 He said that leading candidates for Lagarde's job appeared to be former Netherlands central bank head Klaas Knot and Spain's Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the general manager of the Bank for International Settlements.
 "The European Union is trying to guard itself at least somewhat against the risk that right-wing Marine Le Pen may win the French presidential election in April-May 2027," Schmieding wrote in an email. "Lagarde's successor will still be appointed while the staunchly pro-European centrist Emmanuel Macron still resides in the Elysee Palace."
 Lagarde, the former head of the International Monetary Fund, was appointed in 2011 to succeed Mario Draghi.
